title: unexpected ignore.case = TRUE defaults in starts_with(), ends_with() etc.
description:
I find it unexpected that tidyselect functions like `starts_with()` have `ignore.case = TRUE` as default, so that e.g.
```r
data.frame(ABCDE = 1, abcde = 2) |> 
  select(starts_with("abc"))
```
selects both columns. If you'd ask someone if the string "ABCDE" starts with "abc", I'm sure that the vast majority of programmers would say no because they contain different Unicode characters.

Even more, the documentation of that function does not communicate this point correctly on two occasions:
1) In the description part of the function, it is said 'These match variables according to a given pattern. starts_with(): Starts with an exact prefix.' -> But the prefix is't exact. For a prefix of length n, there are 2^n matches it resolves.
2) The 'Selection language' part of the manual states: 'starts_with("a"): names that start with "a"', which is wrong because it should be 'names that start with "a" or "A"'.

I also find it cumbersome that I always have to write `starts_with('abc', ignore.case = FALSE)` in order to match the actual prefix. Because of all that, please consider to move the default to `ignore.case = FALSE`.

title: `vars_pull()` and `eval_select()` work differently with `all_of()`
description:
See also https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/7720

Alternative solution would be to implement `eval_pull()` and deprecate `vars_pull()` https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/issues/189

``` r
b <- "a"

data <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 2) 

tidyselect::vars_pull(
  names(data),
  tidyselect::all_of(b)
)
#> [1] "b"

tidyselect::eval_select(
  rlang::quo(tidyselect::all_of(b)),
  data
)
#> a 
#> 1
```

This shows up in dplyr's `pull()` and `select()` in weird ways

```r
b <- "a"
dplyr::tibble(a = 1, b = 2) |> 
  dplyr::pull(dplyr::all_of(b))
#> [1] 2
dplyr::tibble(a = 1, b = 2) |> 
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(b)) |>
  dplyr::pull()
#> [1] 1
```

I'm having trouble wrapping my mind around what is happening in the `vars_pull()` case

It's possible `vars_pull()` shouldn't allow `all_of()` or `any_of()` at all? That function is really for returning exactly 1 name, right? And it's likely that with `all_of()` and `any_of()` you can get >1? And it doesn't seem to be working right anyways (i.e. not pulling from the surrounding env)

title: Arithmetic operator `/` not causing an error in eval_select()
description:
The tidyselect vignette (https://tidyselect.r-lib.org/articles/syntax.html#arithmetic-operators) says:

>  Within data-expressions (see Evaluation section), +, * and / are overridden to cause an error.

The operators `^` and `*` do output my expected behavior:
```
mtcars %>% tidyselect:::select_loc(cyl^2)
#> Error in `tidyselect:::select_loc()`:
#> ! Can't use arithmetic operator `^` in selection context.

mtcars %>% tidyselect:::select_loc(cyl*2)
#> Error in `tidyselect:::select_loc()`:
#> ! Can't use arithmetic operator `*` in selection context.
```
However, that is not the case for the `/` operator. Here are a few examples of inconsistent outputs, none of which being `! Can't use arithmetic operator / in selection context.`
```
# EXAMPLE 1 -- error related to something other than the `/` operator
mtcars %>% tidyselect:::select_loc(cyl/20)
#> Error in `tidyselect:::select_loc()`:
#> ! Can't select columns past the end.
#> ℹ Location 20 doesn't exist.
#> ℹ There are only 11 columns.

# EXAMPLE 2 -- no error; returns empty location
mtcars %>% tidyselect:::select_loc(cyl/2)
#> named integer(0)

# EXAMPLE 3 -- no error; returns location
mtcars %>% tidyselect:::select_loc(hp/2)
#> hp 
#> 4

```
While `select` isn't intended to perform any operations, the last example is particularly dangerous for someone originally using `select` and then updating the arguments to perform an arithmetic operation while forgetting to change to `mutate`.
```
# unexpected result
mtcars %>% 
  mutate(expected_hp_by_2 = hp/2) %>%
  select(expected_hp_by_2, hp_by_2 = hp/2) # user confuses mutate for select

```
I would advice emitting an error for all unsupported operators, in order to make it consistent with the current behavior of other operators.

_PS: probably for another issue, but using the `+` operator in `select` throws a different error than `^` or `*`._

title: "matches" misinterprets regular expressions from rex
description:
I see that `tidyselect::matches` has some special code to distinguish different kinds of regular expression. However, this logic seems to be implemented as hard-coded checks for certain classes rather than a generic and methods. Since it doesn't account for the "regex" class from the rex package, it can fail, as demonstrated here:

``` r
library(stringr)
library(rex)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'rex'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stringr':
#> 
#>     regex
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:rex':
#> 
#>     matches
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

## Regular rex class: fails
my_regex <- rex("p" %if_next_isnt% "g")
class(my_regex)
#> [1] "regex"
mtcars %>% select(matches(my_regex)) %>% colnames
#> Warning in grep(needle, haystack, ...): TRE pattern compilation error 'Invalid
#> regexp'
#> Error in `select()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `matches(my_regex)`.
#> Caused by error in `grep()`:
#> ! invalid regular expression '(?:p(?!g))', reason 'Invalid regexp'

## Convert to stringr::regex: works
my_stringr_regex <- stringr::regex(my_regex)
#> Warning in stringr::regex(my_regex): Coercing `pattern` to a plain character
#> vector.
class(my_stringr_regex)
#> [1] "stringr_regex"   "stringr_pattern" "character"
mtcars %>% select(matches(my_stringr_regex)) %>% colnames
#> [1] "disp" "hp"
```

<sup>Created on 2025-09-23 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The short-term fix would seem to be to add "regex" to the list of classes treated specially on this line: https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/blob/main/R/helpers-pattern.R#L152

Long-term, perhaps it's possible to make `matches` a generic?

title: Option for `eval_select(allow_positional = FALSE)`
description:
It would be nice if we had a way to disallow positional tidyselection entirely in some cases.

For example, in tidyr here https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/1541#issuecomment-2435532133, we remove columns generated from `names_from` and `values_from` before evaluating the `id_cols` tidyselection to prevent the user from selecting an ID column that collides with the pivot columns. This works quite well unless you use positions in `id_cols`, in which case the positions you supply don't align with the data frame it is actually evaluated on.

We don't think `id_cols` is a great place to be providing positions anyways, so we'd like to completely turn off the ability to use positional selection here.

We think `allow_positional = FALSE` would affect a few places:
- `all_of()` and `any_of()` technically allow positional inputs, so we'd need a `peek_positional()` helper like we have for `peek_vars()` to dynamically determine if we should disallow them there
- `last_col()` works by position and has the potential to be quite confusing if used as an `id_cols`, so it should probably be completely disallowed. It would also need `peek_positional()`.
- In `walk_data_tree()` we'd check for a `literal` that is a numeric value and error when `allow_positional = FALSE`. Hopefully that catches all cases that aren't selection helpers, because everything recurses through here. Even `1:5`, which does `eval_colon()` and recurses through `walk_data_tree()` with the LHS and RHS.

title: Feature request: classed errors for specific tidyselect errors
description:
A user's attempt at selecting a column can fail for various reasons - currently, there are some (extremely brittle) ways to infer what went wrong.

Briefly, if we wanted to distinguish between these three types of tidyselect errors (mismatch, other evaluation error, empty):

```r
library(rlang)
library(tidyselect)
df <- data.frame(x = 1)

selectors <- exprs(
  mismatch = z,
  error = stop(),
  empty = 
)
```

We know that a mismatch error is classed with a vctrs subscript oob error (as of the most recent update) and also stores the problematic selection in `$i`:

```r
err_mismatch <- catch_cnd(
  eval_select(selectors$mismatch, df)
)
class(err_mismatch)
#> [1] "vctrs_error_subscript_oob" "vctrs_error_subscript"    
#> [3] "rlang_error"               "error"                    
#> [5] "condition"
err_mismatch$parent
#> NULL
err_mismatch$i
#> [1] "z"
```

An error from evaluating the user-supplied expression gets chained, so these errors are distinguished by having a `$parent`:


```r
err_error <- catch_cnd(
  eval_select(selectors$error, df)
)
class(err_error)
#> [1] "rlang_error" "error"       "condition"
err_error$parent
#> <simpleError in eval_tidy(as_quosure(expr, env), context_mask): >
err_error$i
#> NULL
```

Lastly, an empty selection that's promoted to an error with `allow_empty = FALSE` has neither `$i` nor a `$parent`:

```r
err_empty <- catch_cnd(
  eval_select(selectors$empty, df, allow_empty = FALSE)
)
class(err_empty)
#> [1] "rlang_error" "error"       "condition"
err_empty$parent
#> NULL
err_empty$i
#> NULL
```

I fully acknowledge that these are not part of the official API, so I do not mean to build on top of this pattern. Instead, I was hoping that tidyselect could throw more specific, classed errors, where possible. For example, it'd be nice for an empty selection error with `allow_empty = FALSE` to look something like this:

```r
err_empty2 <- catch_cnd(
  eval_select(selectors$empty, df, allow_empty = FALSE)
)
class(err_empty2)
#> [1] "tidyselect_error_disallow_empty" "rlang_error"                    
#> [3] "error"                           "condition"
```

... by adding the `"tidyselect_error_*"` class where the error gets thrown:

https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/blob/fd22cc1dc08bd67fd4501bfad9de67628a35e854/R/eval-walk.R#L128-L132

I realize that this is a non-trivial ask that probably requires a lot of deliberation, but I was curious whether this is within scope / planned to be worked on. Thanks in advance for considering!

title: FR: Error on empty selection `allow_empty = FALSE` has informative class
description:
Many of the `eval_select()` errors have a class that lets you know what went wrong, but not the error you get on an empty selection with `allow_empty = FALSE`. This would be useful if people want to rethrow the error so that the "Must select at least one item" message is more informative in the context of their function, especially to disambiguate the source of the error if there are multiple tidy-select arguments (e.g. rethrow as "Must select at least one country").

``` r
library(tidyselect)
```

title: Support for lazy tibbles
description:
Lazy tibbles currently have two issues with `eval_select()`:

1. They are not a vector so one has to simulate a "dummy" tibble with the appropriate column names, e.g with `dtplyr:::simulate_vars()`.
2. The column types are not generally known which is why `allow_predicates` would make sense: #226

The second point is still a bit annoying when trying to do some general work in a generic, e.g. in `tidyr::nest()` unnamed dots are tried to be named

```r
tidyr::nest <- function (.data, ..., .names_sep = NULL, .key = deprecated()) {
  cols <- enquos(...)
  if (any(names2(cols) == "")) {
    col_names <- names(tidyselect::eval_select(expr(c(...)), .data))
    ...
  }
  UseMethod("nest")
}
```

So, it would be necessary to check the type to figure out whether `allow_predicate` should be `TRUE` or `FALSE`. It might make sense if `tidyselect()` could handle this.

Also see https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/1134

title: Standard, non-nested `c()` expressions trigger error on `.name_spec` specification with tidyhelpers
description:
The help for `eval_select()` (v1.1.1) says that `name_spec` is:
	
>A name specification describing how to combine or propagate names. This is used only in case nested `c()` expressions like `c(foo = c(bar = starts_with("foo")))`. See the name_spec argument of `vctrs::vec_c()` for a description of valid name specs.

However, when using tidyhelpers such as `tidyselect::matches()`, even non-nested `c()` expressions trigger an error:

``` r
library(tidyselect)
x=c(foo="Le")
eval_select(matches(unname(x)), iris)
#> Sepal.Length Petal.Length 
#>            1            3
eval_select(matches(x), iris)
#> Error: Can't merge the outer name `foo` with a vector of length > 1.
#> Please supply a `.name_spec` specification.
```
<sup>Created on 2021-10-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

IMHO, I'd think this is a bug as the name should be ignored in 100% of cases I can think of, but I might miss something. In this latter case, you might want to clarify the documentation.

Also, maybe `?eval_select` could deserve an example of how to use `name_spec`? Even after writing this issue and reading `?vec_c`, it would definitely help me use it if ever need to.

title: where() with NA values
description:
The `where()` function produces relatively uninformative errors when functions output `NA` values. It would be useful for the user if this was checked.

In this example, the function, `~any(str_detect(.x,","))` returns `TRUE` and `FALSE` values, but also returns `NA` values, and so the below throws an uninformative error:
```
gss_cat %>%
  select(where(~any(str_detect(.x,","))))
Error: `where()` must be used with functions that return `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
```

This can be rectified using `na.rm=T` in the `any()` function, as below:
```
gss_cat %>%
  select(where(~any(str_detect(.x,","),na.rm=T)))
```

I believe that having this throw an error is important, as it draw attention to the `NA` values, but since all the values are `logical`, the error should be more informative.

This is also in contrast to the `select_if()` version of this call:
```
gss_cat %>%
  select_if(~any(str_detect(.,",")))
```

which treats `NA` values the same as `FALSE`

However, using this approach, a data frame with 0 columns is returned. I guess that num_range is only suited for full matches, however the help function doesn't say a word about it and I also think num_range would benefit from an option to not only add a prefix, but also a suffix.

```
library(tidyverse)
# Data
df <- data.frame(x1 = c(1, 2),
                 x2 = c(3, 4),
                 x3 = c(5, 6),
                 x4y = c(7, 8),

# 2  2  4  6   8     10     12      14

df %>% select(num_range("x", 1:2) & ends_with("_rec"))

# 1      9     11
```

What I could imagine is really just an extension of the num_range function, e.g.:

```
num_range(prefix = "x",

```

title: Conflict between selection of multiple columns in `last_col()` and _R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_
description:
When you have set `"_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_"` to `TRUE` (which many folks do to guard against accidentally using `&&` for non-scalars), you are no longer able to select multiple columns with `last_col()`.

Here's an example where I select the last three columns of `starwars` by passing in the vector `0:2` as the first argument to `last_col()`. It works fine normally but fails when the environment variable is set to `TRUE`

``` r
library(dplyr)

Sys.setenv("_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_" = FALSE)

starwars %>%
  select(last_col(0:2))
#> # A tibble: 87 x 3
#>    starships vehicles  films    
#>    <list>    <list>    <list>   
#>  1 <chr [2]> <chr [2]> <chr [5]>
#>  2 <chr [0]> <chr [0]> <chr [6]>
#>  3 <chr [0]> <chr [0]> <chr [7]>
#>  4 <chr [1]> <chr [0]> <chr [4]>
#>  5 <chr [0]> <chr [1]> <chr [5]>
#>  6 <chr [0]> <chr [0]> <chr [3]>
#>  7 <chr [0]> <chr [0]> <chr [3]>
#>  8 <chr [0]> <chr [0]> <chr [1]>
#>  9 <chr [1]> <chr [0]> <chr [1]>
#> 10 <chr [5]> <chr [1]> <chr [6]>
#> # ... with 77 more rows
  
Sys.setenv("_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_" = TRUE)

starwars %>%
  select(last_col(0:2))
#> Error: 'length(x) = 3 > 1' in coercion to 'logical(1)'
 ```

<sup>Created on 2020-09-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


And I can see that the source code for `last_col()` uses `&&` in the first condition, which checks that **A)** a number is passed in to the `offset` argument and **B)** this number does not exceed the total number of columns.  This line here seems to be triggering the conflict


https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/blob/7f3b5bb8ac45a355bbe5ace6732bda972fd40eb6/R/helpers-misc.R#L69


If the ability to select multiple columns with a vector in `last_col()` is or can be a feature, may I suggest a change like swapping `&&` with `&` and wrapping the condition in `all()`? This would make the code explicit about the fact that `last_col()` can take a vector of numbers and resolve the conflict with `"_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_"`. And this would still trigger that first condition if any of the numbers in the vector are out of range, so there shouldn't be a problem afaik.

But to be fair to the side of not making a change like this, even with `"_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_"` set to true you still _can_ select multiple columns from the last - it'd just involve more typing:

```
starwars %>%
  select(last_col(0):last_col(2))
```

title: Recode with selection helpers
description:
With the upcoming support for vectors that don't require unique names (e.g. not data frames), we have an opportunity to make `rename()` more useful with select helpers:

```r
levels <- c("foo1", "foo2", "foo3", "bar1", "bar2")

x <- set_names(seq_along(levels), levels)

x
#> foo1 foo2 foo3 bar1 bar2
#>    1    2    3    4    5

rename(x, trt = starts_with("foo"))
#>  trt  trt  trt bar1 bar2
#>    1    2    3    4    5

rename(x, trt = starts_with("foo"), ctrl = starts_with("bar"))
#>  trt  trt  trt ctrl ctrl
#>    1    2    3    4    5
```

This might not be very useful for names, but I think it might be useful for recoding of characters and factors:

```r
chr_relevel(levels, trt = starts_with("foo"))
#> [1] "trt"  "trt"  "trt"  "bar1" "bar2"

chr_relevel(levels, trt = starts_with("foo"), ctrl = starts_with("bar"))
#> [1] "trt"  "trt"  "trt"  "ctrl" "ctrl"
```

Maybe we could even add tidyselect support in `vec_recode()`:

```r
spec <- tibble::tibble(
  .new = c("trt", "ctrl"),
  .old = vars(starts_with("foo"), starts_with("bar"))
)
vec_recode(levels, spec)
#> [1] "trt"  "trt"  "trt"  "ctrl" "ctrl"
```

or I guess more directly:

```r
vec_recode(levels, vars(trt = starts_with("foo"), ctrl = starts_with("bar")))
#> [1] "trt"  "trt"  "trt"  "ctrl" "ctrl"
```

Using tidyselect to recode vectors might require improving efficiency with large n.

We should design name-combination with minimally-named inputs in terms of these potential developments.

title: Can `where(predicate_a | predicate_b)` be supported?
description:
When boolean operators were introduced, they made sense as tidyselect supports the bare functions so we could write:

``` r
select(is.factor | is.numeric)
```

but, now we have to write:

``` r
select(where(is.factor) | where(is.numeric))
```

Looking at https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/issues/106#issuecomment-521521523, `|` and `&` were intended to work only with functions (though now it works just as same as `c()`). So, I feel it's natural that we can use `|` to combine functions directly, though I'm not sure if this change is worth implementing, considering the complexity.

title: A more efficient `&` and `|` ?
description:
See the following example : 

``` r
library(dplyr, w = F)
system.time(
  select(band_members, name & where(~ {Sys.sleep(1); is.character(.)}))
)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.004   0.001   2.011
```

It takes 2 seconds but we know from the `lhs` of `&` that we had a single candidate so it might have taken only 1 second.

I understand that : 
* (1) Tidy selection is usually fast anyway
* (2) `&` is traditionally commutative 

But : 

* (1) tidy selection can be applied on more than data frames and in some cases the conditions that are applied to the data (through where() or custom helpers)  might take time
* (2) we're already redefining `&` to work on numeric values anyway and it would stay functionally commutative (unless we really care about the rhs potentially failing on items dismissed by lhs), users worried about efficiency might just put the expensive condition last.

I don't believe there is an easy way at the moment to compute efficiently `select(data, cheap_selection_1(), cheap_selection_2() & expensive_selection())`

An alternative would be to have `&&` as well, but I think I'd be personally happier with an enhanced `&`.

The same principle apply to `|` and comma separated selections, if a selection is already validated there's no need to go through it again unless it's negative (and then the negated selection should only consider previously selected items).

```
library(dplyr, w = F )
system.time(
  select(band_members, name | where(~ {Sys.sleep(1); is.character(.)}))
)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.009   0.001   2.021

system.time(
  select(iris, Species, Sepal.Length, -where(~ {Sys.sleep(1); is.numeric(.)}))
)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.005   0.000   5.027
```

title: eval_resolve() for partial evaluation
description:
@lionel- and I discussed a potential solution to the following issue:

```r
x <- c("x1", "x2")

wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_variables(y, c(all_of(x), x3)) %>% # <- quosure captured here
  add_model(linear_model)

fit(wf, data) # <- data is here
```

In the above example, `add_variables()` currently has to capture tidyselect expressions as quosures and delay evaluation until `fit()` is called with data. This can potentially result in capturing large environments. tidymodels users often serialize their workflows, which can result in abnormally large objects because of these quosures. recipes has a similar issue.

An alternative is to call a function like `eval_resolve()` from inside `add_variables()`. It would resolve the env-expressions that could be immediately evaluated, and would essentially inline them. It would return a pure expression, rather than a quosure, which workflows could cheaply hold onto until it needs to evaluate the data-expressions in the `fit()` call.

Special env-expressions like `starts_with(foo)` that require some amount of laziness would be handled so that `foo` gets evaluated and inlined, but `starts_with()` itself doesn't. The only env-expressions that require this laziness are native to tidyselect, so Lionel thinks they could all be handled without missing any edge cases.

title: Use anonymous functions in tidy select
description:
Previously in `dplyr`, we could provide predicates to `mutate_if` (and `summarize_if`) like:
```r
iris %>%
  mutate_if(~"virginica" %in% .x, paste0, "_")
#>   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
#> 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa_
#> 2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2 setosa_
#> 3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa_
#> 4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2 setosa_
#> 5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2 setosa_
#> 6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4 setosa_
```
However, scoped verbs like `mutate_if` have been replaced with `across`, which uses the tidy-select framework for variable selection. So the equivalent code is to use an `is_` function:
```r 
is_virgin <- function(x) {
  "virginica" %in% x
}

iris %>%
  mutate(across(is_virgin, paste0, "_"))
```
Or column specification:
```r
iris %>%
  mutate(across(which(sapply(., function(x) "virginica" %in% x)), paste0, "_"))
```
Given that `across` is replacing scoped verbs, including `mutate_if` and `summarize_if`, the ability to use a predicate function would be useful. The former example can be time consuming and confusing when doing multiple `mutate_if` style operations, and the latter is not ideal even for a single use. I think it would be useful to pass in anonymous functions directly, just as the named function can be, in the same syntax as in `mutate_if`. 
```r
iris %>%
  mutate(across(~"virginica" %in% .x, paste0, "_"))
```
I see this isn't likely as it's not able to combine with other tidy select operators, so could this be a use case for a tidy helper that takes anonymous functions and can be combined with other helpers. For lack of a better naming idea, something like `matches_pred`:
```r
iris %>%
  mutate(across(matches_pred(~"virginica" %in% .x), paste0, "_"))
```

title: Inconsistent error for column not found when using rlang with vars_pull
description:
Found as a side-effect of an issue raised whilst building a reprex on tidyr.

We're trying to call tidyselect but specifying a column which is missing (or mis-spelt, or whatever). As a user, you want a friendly error that helps you realise the mistake you've made.

Here we first of all make the mistake using the call directly (in this case our tibble has columns a and b, but we've asked for c). The returned error makes it easy to realise the mistake.

In the second example however we've passed our incorrect column name as a parameter in a function. The end result is a less-friendly error which makes it much harder to realise what the error is.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(rlang)

df <- tibble::tibble(a = 1:2, b = 3:4)

tidyselect::vars_pull(names(df), "c")
#> Error: Strings must match column names. Unknown columns: c

missing_column_demo_fun <- function(df, col) {
  col <- ensym(col)
  tidyselect::vars_pull(names(df), !!enquo(col))
}

missing_column_demo_fun(df, "c")
```

title: rename_all fails on data.frame with dirty names
description:
`rename_all` requires distinct, non-missing variable names in the input data.frame.  This is something of a circular problem for me: I want to use `rename_all` in `janitor::clean_names()` to address https://github.com/sfirke/janitor/issues/260 where grouping indices of a grouped_df are not updated along with the column names.

But the problematic variable names that often go into `clean_names()` are causing `rename_all` to fail.  For instance, with duplicated names, or missing names:

```r
# repeat names
test_df <- as.data.frame(matrix(ncol = 2))
names(test_df) <- c("repeat", "repeat")
test_df %>% rename_all(make.names)
#> `data` must be uniquely named but has duplicate columns

# missing names
test_df <- as.data.frame(matrix(ncol = 2))
names(test_df) <- c("hi", "")
test_df %>% rename_all(make.names)
#> Error in is_symbol(expr): argument "expr" is missing, with no default
```
(I'm using `make.names` to show it's not a `make_clean_names()` problem, but my actual use case would be calling `make_clean_names()`)
 
I welcome advice of all kinds - if there's a way I can get `clean_names()` to update the group names of a grouped_df without using `rename_all` that's great too 😃

```r
library(tidyselect)
```

```r
  env_bind_lazy(data_env, !!!data)
```

After:

``` r
library(tidyselect)
cnames <- paste0("c", 1:100000)

t1 <- proc.time()
x <- vars_select(cnames, "c1")
```

title: select() should warn on factor arguments
description:
The guide on tidy evaluation suggests [forwarding `...` to dplyr functions](https://tidyeval.tidyverse.org/dplyr.html#patterns-for-multiple-arguments) to handle multiple arguments in an NSE setting. In general, this works extremely well and allows custom functions to take advantage of the dplyr flexibility. For example,

``` r
from_mtcars <- function(...) {mtcars %>% select(...)}
from_mtcars( vs, am )              # Automatic quoting of arguments
from_mtcars( starts_with("d") )    # Select helper support
```

Unfortunately, almost invariably somebody passes a factor to the custom function, which leads to unexpected behavior. This usually happens when the user is working with traditional data frames and forgets to do `stringsAsFactors=FALSE`:

``` r
df <- data.frame( v=c("vs","am") )
from_mtcars( df$v )
#                     cyl  mpg
# Mazda RX4             6 21.0
# Mazda RX4 Wag         6 21.0
# ...
```

The behavior is due to factors getting converted to integer indices. This creates hard-to-catch bugs in the end user code, because the conversion is silent and the user usually expects the input to behave as strings. The author of the custom function can add a guard against this:

``` r
from_mtcars2 <- function(...)
{
    v <- purrr::map_if( list(...), is.factor, as.character )
    mtcars %>% select(!!!v)
}
```

Unfortunately, this breaks NSE support:
``` r
# Works as expected with factors
from_mtcars2( factor(c("vs","am")) )
#                     vs am
# Mazda RX4            0  1
# Mazda RX4 Wag        0  1
# ...

# But not with unevaluated expressions
from_mtcars2( mpg )
# Error in map_lgl(.x, .p, ...) : object 'mpg' not found
```

Since `select()` already has low-level access to variables, I was hoping that it could automatically check for the presence of factor arguments. If nothing else, I think that throwing a warning upon encountering one can help alert end users that they are about to encounter unexpected behavior. Potential place where this could be done is around

https://github.com/r-lib/tidyselect/blob/4de95ee641b68f7ab098816d01e02737afa2410c/R/vars-select.R#L144

where character arguments get mapped to integer positions.

title: performance issue of inds_combine with many columns. Could be improve using std::string
description:
Hello,

We noticed that `dplyr::select()` is slow when many columns are supplied. After investigations, @koncina and me, we found that this line Rcpp line might be the one to change:
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyselect/blob/master/src/combine_variables.cpp#L28

The declaration of `out_name` as `<String>` and not `std::string` is slowing down the process.

Historically, it comes from a fix of an encoding issue by @romainfrancois [here](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/commit/e6b1ad5224b6503ff553d1ca21cdba6da65379b7). Later on, @romainfrancois did a second [fix](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/commit/c7c9a6f2ebf89d7fc096aff598040c49a89e99f1) but `String` remains. I must stress out that I know nothing about encoding, so keeping the `String` type could be mandatory.


After replacing L28 by `std::vector<std::string> out_name;` creating a function `inds_combine_std`, we obtained:

```
fake_columns <- paste0("col_", 1:50000)
system.time(v1 <- tidyselect:::inds_combine(fake_columns, list(-1)))
system.time(v2 <- inds_combine_std(fake_columns, list(-1)))
identical(v1, v2)

  user   system elapsed
11.548    0.003  11.556
  user   system elapsed
 0.007    0.000   0.007
 [1] TRUE
```

Of note, this line is also present in the current `dplyr` code:
https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/master/src/combine_variables.cpp#L29

We replaced in `dplyr` v0.7.4 [L29](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/master/src/combine_variables.cpp#L29) with `std::string` and did some benchmark, see how it also improves:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/710181/37719105-8fe707a0-2d24-11e8-8558-2f45223740ae.png)

Is there any (encoding) reason to keep the `String` type in both `tidyselect` and `dplyr`?

title: re-exporting predicate functions
description:
Currently in order to evaluate tidyselect predicates you need to re-export the tidyselect functions, e.g.

```
#' @importFrom tidyselect starts_with
#' @export starts_with
tidyselect::starts_with
```

This doesn't seem problematic by itself, but I'm wondering if this will lead to library symbol conflicts if you are using dplyr and tidyselect, and dplyr is not re-exporting from tidyselect but rather using it's own definitions.

If the plan is for dplyr to migrate to using tidyselect then I think there is no issue. If not, it might be problematic to require the re-export as we'd by inflicting a whole new category of masking problems on users. 

If there is no straightforward way to get dplyr to use tidyselect, one solution that occurred to me is that you *could* automatically make those symbols available to expressions captured by `vars_select` (i.e. they become part of the built-in selection grammar and therefore don't require public visibility/re-exporting).
